title: 'Seismic shift': Māori set to invest in First Nations projects under new deal
text:
Indigenous business groups hope an historic deal with one of the largest and wealthiest tribal authorities in Aotearoa New Zealand will bring much-needed investment in large-scale First Nations projects.

The investment partnership between federal government agency Indigenous Business Australia (IBA) and the Waikato-Tainui iwi (nation) was signed today in Sydney.

Under the deal, IBA will help Waikato-Tainui, which holds around $AU2 billion in assets, invest in projects developed with Traditional Owners, including in the resources and agriculture sectors.

IBA chair Darren Godwell, a proud descendant of the Kokoberren peoples, said the signing of the "letter of intent" between two Indigenous investment institutions was a "seismic shift" for self-determination in Australia.

"We've got Indigenous institutional capacity that's willing to mobilise investment at scale so that TOs [Traditional Owners] can participate in the biggest projects that are happening on their Country," he said.

"Once we ... extend this invitation out to Indigenous Australia, we think we're going to be swamped with demand and opportunities."

Darren Godwell and Tuku Morgan signed the agreement Tuesday morning. (Supplied: Joseph Mayers/IBA)

Waikato-Tainui Chairman Tuku Morgan was in Sydney for the signing and said it represented a "watershed moment".

"This is about trying to build a new era of relationships that promises cohesion, better synergy on the basis of shared values, shared cultural values, shared environmental values, and the ability to do business with each other," he said.

Mr Godwell said the Waikato-Tainui, already a big investor in New Zealand retail, residential, ports and agriculture projects, is looking to generate long-term commercial returns.

He said the iwi is also concerned about being too exposed to the New Zealand economy.

"They need to offset that risk by investing in other places, and what better place to invest than Australia."

IBA's Darren Godwell says the deal is a 'watershed moment' for economic self-determination. (Supplied: Indigenous Business Australia)

The IBA will work closely with the Waikato-Tainui to help ease the transition into Australia, he said.

"We're going to share our information, our market intelligence, and then our relationships directly with TOs."

A 'stepping stone' for more capital investment

While the successful projects are yet to be decided, early beneficiaries could be Indigenous stakes in ports or large-scale renewable projects, as well as industries such as mining, agriculture and botanicals.

Mr Godwell said Yindjibarndi WaterCo's recent agreement to acquire the Dampier Seawater Desalination Plant in the Pilbara from Rio Tinto and the WA government is one contender.

"A large-scale project like that is something that's a very serious proposition for an investment partnership like the one we're announcing."

Michael Woodley hopes the deal will prompt broader interest in First Nations investment opportunities. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

CEO of the Yindjibarndi Group Michael Woodley said the new partnership was an example of First Nations people empowering each other across borders.

"It hasn't been something that First Nations have generally been successful (at) in the past," he said.

"The market as well … will obviously see this as a stepping-stone towards supporting First Nations with capital investment for our ideas."

Mr Woodley said he hoped it would open doors for more global First Nations institutions to do the same.

"Australia is one of the establishing frontiers for First Nations in terms of economic development, economic investment," he said.

"That could lead to something bigger and better in terms of how we unite around the globe."

Many Maori tribal authorities in New Zealand hold investment portfolios funded by historical Treaty of Waitangi settlements, with proceeds distributed to community projects such as social housing, health, environment and education.

"At the heart of what we do is, how do we build and ensure the ongoing prosperity of our people and at the same time, achieve the preservation and ongoing sustenance of the environment [and] keeping our culture alive, our language alive," Mr Morgan said.

The Waikato-Tainui is made up of 100,000 people, including around 15,000 who live in Australia, he said.

"They married into First Nations mobs across Australia. They are part of our family.

"Connecting and doing this high-level agreement is more than just doing business. This is family."

The agreement will be signed again in New Zealand at the annual celebration of the Māori Queen's coronation, expected to be attended by thousands of people next month.

title: Perhaps the answer to my dating woes is to simply tell people who I am
text:
Every time I rejoin Tinder or another dating site, I am faced with the dreaded questions of whether to include my disability in my profile.

Often, I omit the fact and only disclose it after a potential match gets to know me a little.

I would like to say I am still being authentic, but in truth I am not.

I am performing an edited version of myself; the socially acceptable one that platonic and romantic prospects seem to connect with.

It is as if, by only mentioning my interests and goals — l am a foodie, history and art buff, and lover of long conversations — I am using my dating app descriptions to scream: "Look, I am just like you. Don't put me in a box."

l sold my belongings and said goodbye to 'fantasy me' I was tired of trying to live up to an idealised version of myself. So, I decided to do something I had learnt from Marie Kondo: sort my wardrobe into what brought me joy and what didn't.

At other times, I do include it, a disclosure coming from a place of acceptance and tiredness. Tiredness from pretending that I don't have a disability, and after a long time desperately trying to follow the rules of what is "normal" in dating, that in hindsight were not actually written anywhere and enforced by no-one but me.

With this disclosure comes the dreaded, unspoken "please still like me" and the questioning of whether I have characterised my disability in an abled-body-friendly way (not too off-putting?). At the same time the alarm bells are ringing in the back of my mind: "Why am I self-editing to make myself palatable?"

I turned dating into a chore

I never get around to answering that question.

My disability is a part of who I am, but it's not the entirety of who I am. (Supplied: Vanessa Mbeve)

Instead, I start swiping away at potential matches with the alarms still ringing in the background. For every 20 l swipe on l come across a profile of a person with disability and recognise something of myself in their profiles, in their choice of words.

Within 30 minutes I have matches, and right out of the gate I am performing a version of myself while getting to know the other person. Presenting my positives and downplaying my disability as a minor thing. As if to say the essence of who I am is not enough, and that my disability is a point of shame.

Disclosure during the chatting phase is met with a few instant unmatches, dead-end conversations, and the odd forward question: "Does your disability prevent you from being sexually active?"

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

But the vast majority of potential matches I encounter largely seem OK with my disability.

And yet when I meet them in person, the performance continues. I show up in character — not as myself — trying to prove I am "normal" and more than my disability. Instead of saying, "this is who I am and this is where I am at."

Do you have a dating story you would like to share? We'd love to hear from you

I am so busy trying to make potential partners comfortable with my disability that I almost forget the more important questions, like "do I even like this person?".

I am brutally reminded of that reality by my sister. When I described a date as "OK," she answered bluntly, "I don't think you like that guy. Otherwise, you would say he's hot, cute, or something."

In an instant, I get that ugly sinking feeling that I have set myself up for failure again because somewhere along the way, I turned dating into a chore. I stopped asking whether I actually wanted someone, or what my end goal was (marriage, a one-night stand, or something else?) and instead became focused on whether I could convince them to want me.

Do I really need to appeal to everyone?

As a result, I end up doing the exact thing I am trying to avoid: harming others and, above all, myself. I disrespect myself, and in turn I disrespect others by not allowing people to see me and make their own informed decision.

And at end of it all, I am exhausted.

For me, dating apps have, in theory, made dating easier and more accessible in terms of being able to meet people. But of all the people I met, I was genuinely attracted to and compatible with only a handful. So do I really need to appeal to everyone?

I no longer worry about what others think of me Vanessa Mbeve spent more than a decade hiding away from the world, unhappy with the way cerebral palsy affected her. Now, at 26, she's breaking free from self-imposed shackles.

The best date I've had so far this year was with someone who did show up as themselves.

We talked for hours until we were the only people left in the bar, and the staff were desperately waiting for us to leave so they could go home.

Maybe trying to find the perfect words to explain myself is a futile endeavour. My disability is a fixture of who I am, but it is not the entirety of who I am, just like all the other things I include in my dating profile.

Perhaps the answer is not to find a better explanation, but to simply tell people who I am.

My name is Vanessa Mbeve, I am 27 I have cerebral palsy. I am addicted to Cheetos and my laptop. On a weekend you will find me out or blasting music in my house while scrolling on Reddit.

PS; Did I mention I'm single?

Vanessa Mbeve is a New South Wales-based writer with cerebral palsy. She is passionate about exploring social dynamics and sharing her unique perspectives through her writing.

title: Dying woman urges PM to overturn 'cruel' law to save others suffering
text:
As she prepares to die tomorrow using voluntary assisted dying (VAD), Sandra Sarantou has one final request for the prime minister.

She is urging the nation's leaders to change a law that is limiting some Australians' access to VAD.

Sue died before she could access assisted dying Despite voluntary assisted dying being legal in Victoria, many regional patients are not getting the same end-of-life care.

Nine weeks ago, the 58-year-old Adelaide woman was diagnosed with the same aggressive lung cancer her father died from.

Medication is no longer effective for her nerve pain, nausea and dizziness. Having watched her father endure a long and painful death, before VAD was legal around the country, Ms Sarantou is "grateful" to be ending her life on her terms.

But she said she was shocked to learn a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code means some Australians are effectively denied access because of where they live.

"It's even a struggle just to move from one end from the house to another … for those people to travel hours to possibly see a doctor and not get the chance for VAD is just horrific," she told ABC News.

VAD is legal in every Australian jurisdiction except the Northern Territory, which is expected to pass legislation allowing it this month.

Other state laws do allow the use of telehealth for some discussions about VAD, particularly where patients are too ill to travel or live remotely.

But a provision in the Commonwealth Criminal Code, intended to outlaw the use of "carriage services" to "incite suicide", has been interpreted to apply to doctors advising patients about VAD and has overridden those state provisions.

That means doctors cannot use phone, email, internet or video to advise patients about accessing VAD medication.

Workforce shortages in rural and remote areas have meant some dying people have been forced to travel long distances to make those appointments. For some that has not been possible and they have missed out.

Families of people who wanted to access VAD but died before completing the process say telehealth consultations could have spared them unnecessary suffering.

Pressure on the prime minister

Federal Independent Kate Chaney will today attempt to bring on debate of her private members bill, which would see the Commonwealth Criminal Code amended.

Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young will introduce a similar bill to the Upper House this month. Without government support, both bills may languish.

WA MP Kate Chaney has a private member's bill to allow the use of telehealth for VAD consultations. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

There is also a push within Labor's rank and file for change. Last month, delegates to Labor's National Conference voted to amend the party's platform, supporting the use of telehealth for end-of-life care.

Delegates also enshrined a commitment to give Labor MPs and senators a conscience vote on all VAD issues.

Albanese under pressure over telehealth for VAD At the recent Labor conference, only one issue was contested on the floor: support for the use of telehealth in voluntary assisted dying care.

Labor sources have said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese remains personally opposed to allowing telehealth for VAD, and his opposition may prove crucial to the fate of any legislative change.

He supports voluntary assisted dying but has argued face-to-face consultations are an important way to ensure vulnerable patients are not taken advantage of.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has also expressed reservations and raised concerns about the risk of elder abuse if telehealth was allowed.

Several Labor MPs have told the ABC they are confident the law will eventually change but that it will require more time and conversations to convince the prime minister.

Sandra Sarantou had a career as a paramedic, often working in rural areas of South Australia. (Supplied: Sandra Sarantou)

Ms Sarantou, who worked as a paramedic for 13 years and treated patients in rural areas, felt "guilty" she could access VAD while others could not.

"Their time is ticking and they have to suffer. It's cruel, it's not fair," she said.

She is pleading with the Albanese government to amend the criminal code.

"Please change these laws, make it fair and available for everyone despite where they are living."

Doctor: 'It's absolutely an equity issue'

Advocacy group, Go Gentle's latest "State of VAD report" suggested there was strong demand for the care outside cities, with 39 per cent of applicants in 2024-25 living in rural, regional and remote areas.

General practitioner Scott Lewis has travelled 3,000 kilometres across South Australia in the past fortnight alone to see people seeking voluntary assisted dying.

South Australian GP Dr Scott Lewis flies to regional areas of the state to see patients, including those who want to access voluntary assisted dying. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Dr Lewis, who flies his own plane to reach rural patients, said he saw about two new VAD patients a week.

He said workforce shortages and the lack of Medicare funding were preventing more rural doctors from offering VAD care.

"[Rural and remote] doctors are so busy as it is, that they simply haven't had the time or thought to extend their practice into voluntary assisted dying," he said.

"I don't make much money from it, to be blunt."

He told ABC News he had experienced "a sense of failure" knowing patients have missed out on VAD due to their isolation.

"To see the hurt in family members who've had to see their loved ones suffer and … come so close to being approved for voluntary assisted dying but not quite get there … it's hard at times."

A tricky situation

Sydney University Law Health expert Dr Christopher Rudge said he believed telehealth could be allowed without weakening overall protections.

"Across the country the states have very rigorous and documented process for permitting someone to undergo a VAD procedure, and all of those would apply whether it's by telehealth or any other circumstance," he said.

Dr Christopher Rudge, of the University of Sydney Law School. (Supplied)

"My understanding is that the telehealth communications would occur at an early stage of the process but that at some stage, the witnessing and some other processes, would presumably need to occur in an environment where doctors are present."

Generally, under state laws, people applying for VAD must have been diagnosed with a terminal illness and facing death within a year.

They must attend face-to-face medical appointments so that two independent, trained practitioners can assess whether they are eligible, acting voluntarily and capable of making their own decisions.

The patient must provide a written request for VAD, which has to be witnessed by independent adults — not family members.

A co-ordinating practitioner makes a final declaration and a state board — or oversight body — provides final approval.

Dr Rudge said he was "sympathetic" with concerns that telehealth could replace face-to-face consults, but did not think that would be a consequence of changes to the Commonwealth Criminal Code.

"In circumstances where informed consent is not clear, the in-person consultation is the best place for those questions to be answered. And so, I can understand why people could be concerned," he said.

Laughter and legacy

For Sandra Sarantou, the hardest part of preparing for VAD is knowing that she has to say goodbye to her son.

But, she said they had been "completely open" about the VAD process and had found comfort in black humour.

Sandra Sarantou held a party with friends before her planned death through voluntary assisted dying. (Supplied: Sandra Sarantou)

"We had the idea to put my ashes into a big party cracker … and then everybody has got a bit of my ashes," Ms Sarantou laughed.

title: Good Things festival returns in 2026 with big headliner
text:
Having cemented its status as an annual summer festival staple, Good Things has announced its return this December, boasting a line-up packed with metal, punk, emo, rock and more.

The event's seventh edition once again spans a range of genres and eras, bringing together both local and international acts across multiple stages. Let's dive in, shall we?

Who's topping the bill?

Arguably the defining band of nu-metal, Limp Bizkit are back in the country for the first time since headlining Good Things and sideshows back in 2023.

Emerging in the late '90s with a riotous fusion of rock, metal and rap, Limp Bizkit's angsty anthems were a polarising force but became a blockbuster success with teenage millennials.

Fronted by Fred Durst, songs like Nookie, Break Stuff, Rollin, and Mission: Impossible 2 theme Take A Look Around, were inescapable in the 2000s.

Limp Bizkit were also never far from headlines; most famously, their 2001 performance at the Sydney Big Day where 16-year-old Jessica Michalik died.

'I had her hand, then I let it go': the Big Day Out loses its innocence A confluence of factors during Limp Bizkit's 2001 Sydney performance led to the death of 16-year-old Jessica Michalik. Eighteen years later, the anger and the hurt remain.

At 2012's Soundwave festival, the band's first Australian dates in 11 years, Durst dedicated their performance to Jessica and was joined by her father, George Michalik.

Heavy fans will be thrilled to experience Spiritbox. Fronted by Courtney LaPlante, a vocalist capable of ethereal melodies and visceral screams, the Canadian metal group boldly mixed genre on their breakout 2020 debut album Eternal Blue.

Between that record and last year's acclaimed follow-up, Tsunami Sea, Spiritbox have been feted in just about every way that still matters: magazine covers, festival billings, a ferociously dedicated fanbase and multiple nominations at Canada's Juno music awards.

This marks Spiritbox's second time touring Australia, following their 2023 debut as part of Knotfest. (Supplied: Alexander Bemis)

Simple Plan, Montreal's premiere pop-punk exports and a staple of 2000s, are also at the top of the bill. Nearly 30 years after forming, the band still largely consists of the same high school friends, who've released six albums much loved by anyone who went through an emo phase in the 2000s.

Alexisonfire, yet another celebrated Canadian act, will mark the 20th anniversary of Crisis, their influential third album of bracing post-hardcore, by performing the record in full.

Similarly, Swedish punk group Millencolin will perform their 2000 album Pennybridge Pioneers — an international hit evidenced by its songs featuring in the blockbuster Tony Hawk's Pro Skater video games, as well as Penguins & Polarbears cracking triple j's Hottest 100.

What about Aussie acts?

The biggest homegrown heavy name is resilient metalcore crew Polaris, who are beginning work on new material to follow their first three ARIA-nominated albums.

Grinspoon, who've been touring rock favourites since the late '90s, are sure to draw big sing-alongs. Their addition follows frontman Phil Jamieson cancelling his current tour after a serious back injury sustained mid-show.

You've also got Speed, the J Award-winning crew who put Western Sydney's hardcore scene on international radars with their community-driven live shows.

Loading Instagram content

Plus, Slowly Slowly, who've hopped from emo-rock to pop-punk and even glossy electro-pop, Brisbane four-piece Headwreck and the Choirboys.

Best known for their 1987 pub rock hit Run To Paradise, the Choirboys fill a legacy slot that has become Good Things tradition, occupied in previous years by James Reyne and Dragon.

Who else is playing?

Bad Religion, pioneers of a melodic take on hardcore that helped draft the blueprint that '90s acts like Green Day and The Offspring drafted from, are billed to celebrate their "45 + 1 year anniversary."

The All-American Rejects will bring their alt-rock and pop--punk songbook to Australia for the first time in over 17 years, after having to pull out of last year's Good Things festival.

There's also The Devil Wears Prada, the Ohio metal group who, like the popular 2006 movie, take their name from the 2003 bestselling novel.

Industrial metal trailblazers Ministry will make Good Things the Australian stop of their global farewell tour, ending a 45-year career.

Ringleader Al Jourgensen has stated he's "f***ing done" after Ministry's final live shows and upcoming 17th album Hate To Go (Take Out or Delivery). (Supplied: Derick Smith)

Other Good Things acts include Christian nu-metal group P.O.D, Mudvanye and Hellyah vocalist Chad Gray; Bilmuri, aka US singer-songwriter John Franck; punk rock mainstays MxPx and Welsh pop-punk band Neck Deep.

Plus, there's German trio Future Palace; young internet sensation ivri; dynamic singer-drummer Kami Kehoe; and Voice of Baceprot, an all-female Muslim Indonesian heavy metal trio.

Here's the full Good Things line-up so far:

Limp Bizkit, Simple Plan, Spiritbox, Polaris, The All-American Rejects, Bad Religion, Alexisonfire, Grinspoon, Millencolin, Ministry, Bilmuri, Chad Gray, MxPx, Neck Deep, Speed, Slowly Slowly, P.O.D., The Devil Wears Prada, Choirboys, All Them Witches, The Black Queen, Future Palace, Headwreck, The Home Team, House of Protection, ivri, Kami Kehoe, Locked Shut, LØLØ, Vianova, Voice Of Baceprot

Here are the dates, and the festival is once again welcoming younger moshers:

Fri 4 December — Flemington Racecourse: Melbourne, Wurundjeri Woi Worrong Land, VIC (15+)

Sat 5 December — Sydney Showgrounds: Sydney, Gadigal Land, NSW (16+)

Sun 6 December — Brisbane Showgrounds: Brisbane, Turrbal Jagera Land, QLD (16+)

Tickets are on sale from 10am AEST, Thursday August 20. You'll find more info at the Good Things website.

title: Potholes force cars off Calder Freeway as Victorian road anger rises
text:
More drivers have been left stranded after their vehicles were damaged by a pothole on a major Victorian freeway this morning.

Macedon Ranges resident John told ABC Central Victoria, at least seven cars with damaged tyres were lined up on the side of the Calder Freeway between Gisborne and Sunbury about 6.30am.

He said another three were pulled over on the off-ramp.

"There were people changing tyres on the side of the road; one young lady was in tears because she didn't know what to do," he said.

" The same pothole was fixed one week ago. Clearly they're not fixing them adequately. "

He lanes have been closed due to road damage on the freeway between Kyneton and Sunbury for two weeks.

"They're just filling gaps, they're not actually going to the cause of the problem," he said.

"We just keep blaming the weather without proper remediation."

A spokesperson from the Department of Transport couldn't confirm how many vehicles had been affected.

The right lane of the freeway remains closed city-bound near Mundy Road, with patching works under way.

Elsewhere in central Victoria, Johnny Ravet from Seymour Tyre and Mechanical told ABC Statewide Mornings there were six cars in his workshop all with pothole damage.

"Just last week we had one, an Audi, travelling to Nagambie, hit a pothole and no spare tyre so it was towed in," he said.

"That rim [cost] $4000 before we even put a tyre on it."

This morning's traffic hazard on the Calder Freeway follows a similar problem on the Princes Freeway at Bunyip, east of Melbourne yesterday where about 30 cars suffered tyre damage by hitting a pothole that was hard to see in the rain.

title: 'Evidence is clear': Players association says brutal schedule behind injuries
text:
The Professional Tennis Players Association (PTPA) believes a string of withdrawals from the Canadian Open underscore concerns that professional tennis's lengthy calendar and expanded top-level events are increasing injury risks.

The players' advocacy group said it was saddened but not surprised by the absences from the tournament, arguing that reduced recovery time between tournaments was contributing to injuries occurring earlier in the season and becoming more serious.

The Canadian Open men's event in Montreal was hit by the withdrawals of world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time grand slam champion Novak Djokovic, while Carlos Alcaraz was also sidelined with a wrist injury. Hometown favourite Felix Auger-Aliassime also pulled out due to a back injury before his opening match.

On the women's side, defending champion Victoria Mboko, Wimbledon finalist Karolina Muchova, Emma Raducanu and Jasmine Paolini are also missing the tournament with injuries.

The first quarterfinal matches of the tournament begin later on Tuesday AEST.

Tournament organisers said last month that recurring late withdrawals from Masters 1000 events had become a wider issue for the sport.

PTPA says 'evidence is clear'

The PTPA said it had collected and analysed injury data from more than 30,000 professional matches across all levels of the game over the past eight years in a project launched three years ago with its medical director, Dr Robby Sikka.

'Not ready to compete': Sinner pulls out of tournament ahead of US Open Men's tennis world number one Jannik Sinner pulls out of the Cincinnati Open with a right knee injury, handing the Italian a blow in his preparations for this month's US Open.

"The evidence is clear: the season is too long, recovery time is shrinking, and injuries are occurring earlier and becoming more severe," the PTPA said in a statement posted on social media.

The group said upper-body injuries were up 42 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, according to its analysis. Arm injuries were up 112 per cent this year compared with the 2025 average, it added.

The ATP expanded seven of its nine Masters 1000 tournaments to 12-day events under its OneVision strategic plan, with 2025 the first season in which the longer format was used across those events.

The PTPA said the change had cut into the time players have to rest, train and travel between tournaments, despite players having voiced concerns about the demands of the schedule for years.

"Short-term commercial interests cannot come at the expense of player health," the association said. "Protecting players isn't just about today's competitors, it is about protecting the future of tennis."

Schedule the players' choice

The ATP has previously said players retain choices over their schedules and that it is working to create incentives for an appropriate number of matches to be played during the season.

Spokespeople for the ATP and WTA Tours did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The PTPA called for the sport to take a player-health and data-driven approach to restructuring the calendar.

It said players should have a meaningful role in shaping the schedule, while mandatory tournament commitments should be reduced to allow adequate recovery.

It also urged the ATP to consider reversing the 12-day Masters 1000 format.

title: Why Trump selling early access to his posts is causing controversy
text:
US President Donald Trump knows the world hangs on his every word.

A single social media post about tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or oil production can send stocks, commodities and currencies surging or plunging within seconds.

Now, Trump's media company wants to sell some investors a head start.

Investors have reacted sharply to Donald Trump's announcements on tariffs, sanctions, military action and energy policy. (AP Photo: Ahn Young-joon)

Earlier this month, the Trump Media & Technology Group (TMTG), which owns the Truth Social platform, launched a premium data service known as the Truth Social API.

The company says subscribers can receive posts from selected high-profile accounts, including Trump's, within "milliseconds".

According to Reuters, subscriptions cost between $US60,000 ($AU84,930) and $US100,000 ($AU141,550) per month, with several trading firms already signing up.

The move has sparked legal and ethical questions, including whether it is appropriate for a company majority-owned by the sitting US president to profit from selling faster access to his market-moving statements.

But some researchers say there may be an even bigger concern, with data they describe as "extremely suspicious" suggesting some traders could already be receiving information well before Trump's posts appear publicly.

Who is the service for?

To most people, a few milliseconds of early access sounds meaningless.

But modern financial markets increasingly move at computer speed rather than human speed, QUT Digital Media Research Centre associate professor Stephen Harrington says.

Many of the world's biggest trading firms use high-frequency trading, with algorithms buying and selling shares in fractions of a second.

Donald Trump appears on a trader's screen on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. (AP Photo: Richard Drew)

"The only groups that are going to afford to subscribe to that service, and get a genuine advantage out of it, are high-frequency traders," Dr Harrington says.

At least five trading firms have signed up so far, according to The Wall Street Journal.

For companies trading billions of dollars every day, Dr Harrington says a $US100,000 monthly subscription is simply another business expense.

"Getting even the slightest advantage, even when it comes down to just fractions of a second, can be useful."

Does Trump stand to profit?

Trump's family remains the controlling shareholder in Trump Media through a trust, meaning he could benefit financially if the company generates more revenue.

According to the Associated Press, shares in the Truth Social parent company have fallen by 75 per cent since Trump returned to office last year.

The Truth Social platform is owned by Trump Media and Technology Group (TMTG).

Despite Trump's continued use of the platform to announce major policy decisions, Trump Media has continued reporting hundreds of millions of dollars in losses.

"Truth Social is essentially a scam," Dr Harrington says.

"The whole thing was set up not as a legitimate business, but potentially as a way to funnel money to Donald Trump rather than any serious money-making venture in the first place."

Is it illegal?

Finance researcher Dewan Rahman, from the University of Queensland's Business School, says whether the arrangement is unlawful depends on exactly what subscribers are receiving.

If the service simply delivers Trump's posts to paying customers a few milliseconds faster after they have already been published, then it is not illegal.

"If you're paying for speed rather than information, then that's fine," Dr Rahman says.

"The insider trading concern comes when you have an information advantage."

He says premium market data feeds that deliver public information in machine-readable formats within milliseconds are already common across financial markets.

The critical question, Dr Rahman says, is whether subscribers are also obtaining advance knowledge that a market-moving announcement is coming.

"If someone has private information beforehand, or even an indication that an announcement is coming, that's where the concern begins," he says.

"So we need to know those things and it's a question for investigation later on."

Dr Rahman says any evidence that politically connected firms received advance warning of presidential announcements would raise significant insider trading concerns.

Trump is not shy of collecting spoils The US president's most-recent filings indicate he pocketed more than $US2.2 billion last year through ventures ostensibly run by his family.

The service also raises ethical questions, Dr Harrington says.

"When we see a post on Truth Social, how do we know if that's informing the American people and everyone else in the world, or acting in his own financial interests?" he says.

"Public pronouncements by a sitting president should go out to everyone equally at the same time. There shouldn't be a sellable tier where people get that information first."

The White House did not respond to media requests for comment, but Trump has previously rejected criticism of his financial dealings.

Last month, he defended making about $US1.2 billion from cryptocurrency ventures in 2025, saying "everybody is profiting" from the stock market's gains since he returned to the White House.

A CNN/SSRS poll released in late July found 64 per cent of respondents believed Trump had gone too far in pursuing personal financial interests while in office.

Do Trump's posts really move markets?

Like any US president, Trump's public statements can move markets because they often signal changes to government policy or major geopolitical events.

Investors have reacted sharply to his announcements on tariffs, sanctions, military action and energy policy, while oil prices are particularly sensitive to developments in the Middle East.

But Dr Harrington says his team's latest research, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, points to something more unusual.

In one instance, QUT researchers found there was a sudden flurry of movement in the oil market about 20 minutes before Trump's post. (Supplied: QUT)

After analysing market activity surrounding Trump's Truth Social posts over a 73-day window, the researchers found 15 instances in which oil markets appeared to move before he posted on the topic.

In some cases, trading activity increased several minutes before the posts became public.

The researchers cannot say for certain why this happened or who was responsible, but Dr Harrington says the statistical pattern is difficult to dismiss as coincidence.

"It looks extremely suspicious," he says.

"What it seems like is that there are trades being placed by someone with inside information about what the president is about to say in the hour or two leading up to him posting on Truth Social."

Dr Harrington cautions the findings alone cannot prove insider trading is taking place, but says the repeated pattern suggests there may be a more sophisticated strategy at play.

"In reality, the milliseconds [advantage] aren't really the secret sauce," he says.

"If someone is getting information many minutes beforehand, that's where the real money is being made."

title: First look at designs for new Town Hall Square 'in the heart' of Sydney
text:
New renders of what Sydney's new Town Hall Square will look like have been released, promising "the grandeur of a European square".

The new public square will be opposite Town Hall in the heart of Sydney's CBD and the design shows a plaza surrounded by a curved grove of 30 native Australian trees.

Fixed and movable chairs and tables are set to be included in the more than 4,500 square metres of accessible open space.

The City of Sydney has allocated $150 million to the project. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

A European nod

Speaking to 702 ABC Sydney on Tuesday, Lord Mayor of Sydney Clover Moore said the design had "the gravitas and grandeur of a European square" while maintaining Australian charm.

"It's going to be intrinsically Australian and Sydney because instead of [European] columns, it's going to be beautiful gum trees," she said.

" It should be a great gift for Sydney. "

Clover Moore says Town Hall Square will have a European feel to it. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

A key part of the design drawing the ire of some Sydneysiders is the plan to demolish the Woolworths block and six other buildings opposite Town Hall to create the space to build the new square.

City of Sydney Council said most business tenancies in the seven buildings were expected to relocate to alternative premises.

The Woolworths building at Town Hall will be demolished to make way for the new square. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

In response, Cr Moore said none of the buildings that were being removed were of heritage value.

"I think one of the good things about it also is that when those buildings are removed, people are then going to be able to have a really good view of the very beautiful heritage buildings; the Town Hall, Queen Victoria Building, St Andrew's Catheral and Pitt Street Church.

"So it will create an opportunity to have a lovely precinct, sandstone precinct, for those great buildings there."

Cr Moore said the ultimate aim of the square was for it to be a gathering point for the community, and a space for markets, festivals, cultural, music and live sports watching events.

Decades in the making

Sydney's Town Hall in the 1980s. (Supplied: City of Sydney Archives)

The square has been part of Sydney CBD's urban vision since the early 19th century, with successive lord mayors acquiring land on George and Park streets for the project since the 1980s.

There was extensive community consultation in 2007 as part of the council's long-term strategic plan, with the concept of public squares garnering strong support.

The council then resolved to move ahead with the design and construction of Town Hall Square in February, with an unanimous decision made to fast-track demolition work.

$150 million was budgeted in City of Sydney's long-term financial plan, with demolition set for 2028 and the project expected to be completed by 2031.

NSW Premier Chris Minns, however, questioned the cost, saying council needed to justify the large expense.

"It's a matter for them but its very expensive, and like any government you've got an obligation to explain how you'll fund a big project like that and what will be done or not done at its expense," he said on Tuesday.

An artist's impression of what the new square at Town Hall would look like. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

Margy Osmond, chief executive officer of the Tourism and Transport Forum, said the square would attract visitation.

"This is fantastic for Sydney's visitor economy and a once-in-a-generation opportunity to create a new landmark in the heart of the city," she said.

"It has the potential to change the way people experience this part of the city, drawing more visitors and encouraging them to stay longer and spend more, which in turn will attract more investment into the surrounding precinct."

City of Sydney Council said they would give the square a First Nations name.

A development application for Town Hall Square will be lodged in the coming months, to allow Sydneysiders to provide feedback on the design.

title: Bird flu drives a 50 per cent cost increase for badminton players
text:
While bird flu has only landed on Australian shores in the last few months, a group of sportsmen and women have been feeling its impact for years.

The deadly strain of H5 avian influenza has riddled wild and domesticated avian species across the world, with the total number of dead birds in the hundreds of millions.

While the spread of the disease has Australians across science and agriculture increasingly concerned, the nation's badminton players have long counted its costs.

The mass culling of flocks of geese and poultry across east and central Asia in recent years has massively cut the global supply of feathers critical to making the shuttlecocks needed for any game of the racquet sport to go ahead.

Countries across the world have culled birds to manage H5N1 outbreaks. (Reuters: Luc Gnago)

Shuttlecock shock

The impact has seen equipment costs skyrocket for badminton clubs across the country.

A high-quality shuttlecock uses 16 feathers from the left wing of either a duck or a goose, though each bird can only supply two to three feathers that meet specifications.

China is home to most of the world's poultry farms where the specific feathers are harvested, leaving the product exposed to major price fluctuations pinned to the health of the birds.

Goose feathers are at a premium as healthy flocks become rarer. (ABC Great Southern: Eliza Kavanagh)

Badminton Australia chief executive Tjitte Weistra says even a mid-range shuttle, such as the Yonex AS-30, has become near-unaffordable for most players and clubs.

"A decade ago a tube of a dozen AS-30s would sit from $30 to $35. That's now well over $70," he said.

"This means the cost of hosting a tournament or even club play can get very, very expensive."

Tjitte Weistra said synthetic shuttles are not yet good enough for most players. (Supplied: Tjitte Weistra)

Great Southern Badminton Association chair Michelle Watson said her organisation spends $3,000 on shuttles every four to six months.

Nightly fees have had to rise to maintain quality equipment with synthetic alternatives not an option.

Michelle Watson (right) says increasing costs have been challenging for local players. (Supplied: Michelle Watson)

"Feathers are what the game should be played with and are far superior," she said.

"Players that understand the game and play more than at a social level expect quality shuttles.

" I believe synthetics will be the way of the future due to feathers being unsustainable [but] they are currently not close to where they need to be to be an appropriate option. "

WA players particularly hard-hit

Metamorph Shuttle director Ryan Zengyuan said WA's near-total reliance on imported equipment left local players even more exposed.

"An agricultural supply crash in Asia instantly triggers inventory shortages and doubles prices for local players," Mr Zengyuan said.

"[As a result] local sport retailers have been forced to increase retail prices by 30 to 50 per cent over the last few years to cover the skyrocketing cost of raw feathers and international freight."

Players say you cannot replicate the flight of natural feather shuttles. (ABC Great Southern: Will Corbett)

While bird flu has decimated the global feather market, freight costs, oil prices and competition for the cork used in the head of the shuttle are additional factors in the rising prices.

Seeking alternatives

Mr Weistra said local clubs are starting to look at alternative options to curb the price rise, including players making peace with synthetic shuttles.

"They're trying to get cheaper feather shuttles which don't have the same characteristics," he said.

" In the past, they just weren't open to it because the crisis wasn't big enough. But now the cost is becoming really prohibitive. "

"I guess they are inclined to look at alternative options and accept that maybe they're not perfect, but it will do for now."

title: Ben Jones, who played Cooter in the Dukes of Hazzard, has died
text:
Ben Jones, who played the good ol' boy mechanic in The Dukes of Hazzard TV series and parlayed his fame into a political career and two terms in the US House of Representatives, has died.

He was 84.

Jones had a heart attack in his home on Sunday in Washington, Virginia, as he was waiting to watch his beloved Atlanta Braves play baseball, his wife, Alma Viator, said on social media.

From Dukes of Hazzard to House of Reps

Jones's fame came from his role as Cooter Davenport, the mechanic who got the Duke boys out of jams as they tried to fight the corrupt Boss Hogg in the fictional Hazzard County, Georgia.

After playing Cooter for all seven seasons of the series from 1979 to 1985, Mr Jones turned to politics and was elected for the Democrats to the US House from a district near Atlanta in 1988.

He served two terms.

Ben Jones, second from right, with The Dukes of Hazzard cast, from left, Denver Pyle, Catherine Bach, John Schneider and Tom Wopat.

Jones was born in North Carolina.

While he attended college he became involved in acting and civil rights, he wrote in his autobiography Redneck Boy in the Promised Land: The Confessions of 'Crazy Cooter'.

Acting took over his life.

Jones performed in numerous stage productions and had a few minor TV and movie roles in Atlanta during the 1970s before his life-defining break came on a TV show Jones defended as a modern-day morality tale and a fine example of Southern values.

For seven seasons, Jones was one of a small band of friends and family helping Bo and Luke Duke in The Dukes of Hazzard.

The brothers were on probation for running moonshine and were constantly trying to clear their names and stop the crooked and powerful Boss Hogg from stealing or cheating.

The Duke boys drove a modified 1969 Dodge Charger called the General Lee with a Confederate flag on its roof.

Cooter owned Cooter's Garage in the town square.

New Waylon Jennings album released Shooter Jennings unearthed a treasure trove of unreleased recordings from his legendary father Waylon.

Nearly every episode involved a car chase with jumps and stunts and a patrol car badly in need of repairs.

Cooter was often on the CB radio in his pickup truck saying: "Breaker one, Breaker one. I might be crazy but I ain't dumb. Crazy Cooter coming at you."

The Dukes of Hazzard was a hit for CBS and its popularity never waned.

It went into syndication and later became a prominent fixture on cable's The Nashville Network.

Jones also credited the series with pulling him out of a self-destructive, alcoholic lifestyle that led to the failure of several marriages.

"It was like being in a Beatles movie," Jones said.

"Our lives changed."

Tom Wopat, who played Luke Duke, said Jones was an integral part of making the series work.

"Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business. He will be sorely missed," Wopat wrote on Instagram.

A Democrat who could buck his party

After The Dukes of Hazzard, Jones went into politics.

He kept his 'aw shucks' personality, but took the issues seriously.

In his four years in Washington, Jones was known as a Democrat who could buck his party.

He was liberal on social issues and conservative on economics.

But even in politics, he made a splash.

Ben Jones was elected for the Democrats but was prepared to vote against party lines. (AP: Joe Holloway Jr)

After losing in 1992 when the boundaries to his district were redrawn, Jones ran for Congress again in 1994.

He lost to Newt Gingrich in the elections that elevated the Republican to the Speaker's office.

Jones would file an ethics complaint that Mr Gingrich used tax-deductible donations to fund his partisan college course leading to a House reprimand and Mr Gingrich's decision to leave the body.

Jones always embraced his role as Cooter.

After moving to Virginia, he opened at least three Cooter's country stores in Nashville and Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, and near his home.

They sold T-shirts, key chains and insulated tumblers and included Dukes of Hazzard memorabilia like one of the 300 or so General Lee cars used and abused in the TV series.

The show and Cooter lived on because it was funny, had plenty of action and car chases and had a good, family-friendly heart, Jones told the Richmond Times-Dispatch at a 2001 car show, when he played in a band, signed autographs and met fans.

"The show reflects the values of the heartland of America. The good guys always win," Jones said.

AP

title: Kwinana is preparing for a once-in-a-generation rebuild and years of disruption
text:
It is 6am and truck driver Carolus Broers is standing outside a fuel depot in Perth's south with a service-station coffee in hand.

It is here in Kwinana where the city's petrol passes through before being delivered to pumps across the metropolitan area.

Carolus jumps in his tanker and hits the road bound for his first stop — a service station in Ascot, less than 50 kilometres away.

Carolus Broers prepares his truck for a trip across Perth. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

Within minutes he is stationary.

The truck crawls onto the Kwinana Freeway, where traffic has already ground to a halt. It is not peak hour. It is barely 7am.

It doesn't take long for traffic to grind to a halt. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

For the next 45 minutes, the truck struggles to reach 20km/h.

For hundreds of truck drivers moving fuel, fertiliser and waste in and out of Kwinana, this is the daily reality.

And it's about to get worse.

Traffic banked up on the Kwinana Freeway near Anketell Road in Perth's south. (ABC News)

Kwinana is on the cusp of its biggest transformation in decades. The region will become home to AUKUS submarine support facilities and a defence manufacturing precinct, while nearby Westport will become the state's future container port.

Supporting that vision will require billions of dollars in new infrastructure, including a $1.1 billion upgrade of Anketell Road and a $700 million widening of the Kwinana Freeway. Construction is expected to begin early next year.

The state government has been touting its $700 million upgrade of the Kwinana Freeway. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

'Unrecognisable'

The Kwinana Industry Council's David Harrison said the region will be "completely unrecognisable" in a few years.

David Harrison says it's critical Kwinana is able to function as efficiently as possible. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"We are gearing up for the largest infrastructure transformation in Kwinana's history," he said.

"This is off the charts. We have never seen anything like it and we have never done anything like it.

"We're looking at probably a decade or more of infrastructure upgrades. It's not going to be quick or easy."

The government is also spending hundreds of millions of dollars upgrading Anketell Road to be the main gateway to Perth's new container port. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

The challenge, he said, is keeping Kwinana moving while it is rebuilt. The region is the industrial heart of the state.

"The fuel for your cars comes out of Kwinana. The fertiliser to grow our food comes out of Kwinana. Even the oxygen going into our public hospitals comes out of Kwinana," Mr Harrison said.

Kwinana is set for an overhaul with the arrival of the AUKUS submarine project. (ABC News: Mitchell Edgar)

"These roads are the arteries of industry. They have to continue to function."

Meanwhile the US Navy expects up to 2,300 Americans to call Perth's southern suburbs home by 2030.

Defence Minister Richard Marles said it was part of a rotational force to support the AUKUS nuclear submarine based at HMAS Stirling.

Federal politicians are known to frequent HMAS Stirling for announcements when travelling west. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"It's 1,200 personnel, there are civilians, contractors and families, which make up the larger number," he told reporters on Friday.

The premier said more than six-billion dollars of construction work will take place ahead of the American influx, beginning next year.

Planning ahead

Waste company Veolia runs around 200 trucks a day collecting kerbside rubbish before taking it to Kwinana's landfill and waste-to-energy facilities.

WA Municipal Manager Rebecca Goodwin said the company was already planning for heavier congestion by rostering extra drivers and trucks.

Rebecca Goodwin says her company is already planning for the disruption. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

"The impact is large. It is something we are planning for," she said.

" We expect we will need at least another two trucks operating in that southern corridor … just to make sure we can get everybody's bins collected on time. "

Those extra trucks come at a cost, one Veolia hopes it will not have to pass on to councils and ratepayers.

Fuel distributor Atlas Fuels faces the same problem.

Operations executive Tina Hopkins said longer journeys meant more trucks, more drivers and higher operating costs.

Tina Hopkins says her company will be impacted by the delays. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"We have to have extra trucks and extra drivers to manage the deliveries we need to do," she said.

The state government has warned commuters to expect average delays of about 15 minutes while freeway upgrades are underway.

Test of patience

For freight operators, however, those delays quickly multiply across dozens of vehicles and hundreds of deliveries.

By the time Carolus pulls into the Ascot service station, he's been behind the wheel for an hour and 45 minutes.

Carolus Broers says the traffic is a serious issue. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

They're already more than half an hour behind schedule and the major roadworks have not even begun.

It's a glimpse of what lies ahead as Kwinana embarks on a once-in-a-generation rebuild.

It marks the start of years of construction to support WA's industrial future, and a daily test of patience for the people who keep it running.

Carolus Broers stuck in traffic while driving along the Kwinana Freeway. (ABC News: Rick Rifici)

title: Yarning circles raise concerns about repetition of Stolen Generations
text:
Some carers say Stolen Generations history is repeating itself with the number of children in South Australia under the Department for Child Protection (DCP).

A series of yarning circles to collect feedback from carers has heard staffing issues and delays in medical assessments were hindering progress for Aboriginal children in state care.

South Australia has the second highest rate of children in out-of-home care (OOHC) in the nation and almost 40 per cent, or 1,785, of those children are Aboriginal.

The Aboriginal-led organisation KWY has created a four-year research project called Wilto Willo (meaning "spring star" in Kaurna language) to investigate community-led solutions to reduce the over-representation of Aboriginal children in care.

Yarning circle participants made weavings to place at local DCP offices. (Supplied: KWY Adelaide)

About 200 carers have provided feedback through yarning circles at Port Lincoln, Port Augusta and Adelaide.

KWY research and development senior manager Rebecca Cort said the next phase would focus on yarning circle peer-led solutions.

"We have a really big problem in Australia of over-representation [of Aboriginal children in care] and it's growing," Ms Cort said.

"We know that it's growing since last year, so the problem despite all the policy, despite the investment, despite the agreement on closing the gap, the numbers are still worsening."

Rebecca Cort is the senior manager of research and development at KWY Adelaide. (Supplied: KWY Adelaide)

One of the key focus areas was the need to tackle child protection earlier.

"Australia nationally spends about $15 billion a year in child protection and family support — 84.1 per cent of that investment is looking … at intervening after harm has occurred for children and families," Ms Cort said.

Residential care

Children in SA are almost four times more likely to live in residential care than children nationally, with 772 children, or 17.2 per cent, of all OOHC placements in the outmoded type of care.

This is out of step nationally according to 2026 monitoring of the Productivity Commission's Report on Government Services by SA's Guardian for Children and Young People.

"[It] raises serious questions about whether the system is adequately prioritising children's rights to safe family-based care in their community," the report stated.

The rate of Aboriginal children in care in South Australia was 88.6 per 1,000 Aboriginal children in the total care population, compared with 62.4 nationally.

The report stated South Australia continued to fail Aboriginal children at scale despite incremental improvements.

Evelyn Walker says staffing issues have left children without case workers for six months. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Port Lincoln carer Evelyn Walker said there were several issues raised at the local yarning circles about the Department for Child Protection.

These included a large turnover of staff, a fly-in fly-out workforce, staff shortages, a lack of communication and delays in accessing assessments, she said.

Ms Walker said the lack of a permanent and stable workforce left some children and care families without a support worker for six months, and some children had not accessed a psychologist or been assessed to ensure they were on the right medications.

She said some staff did not understand or adhere to Aboriginal placement principles.

"Some children being in non-First Nations placements didn't have connection with their families and even with their culture and going out on country — that's all part of wellbeing," Ms Walker said.

Yarning circle sessions heard concerns about children losing touch with their culture. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"We have had some children that appear to have lost their identity of who they are.

"They don't know their cultural background, they don't know their family connections, they don't know story to country, haven't been on country."

Part of Ms Walker's childhood was spent growing up in another family.

"I can say from my experience when I reconnected back with family, it was very overwhelming … however, it was the best thing for my wellbeing," she said.

Department for Child Protection chief executive Jackie Bray said DCP sought to improve outcomes for Aboriginal children by drawing on the advice of Aboriginal colleagues and community members.

Jackie Bray is the chief executive of SA's Department for Child Protection. (ABC News)

"We have a strong focus on embedding family-led decision-making in our everyday practice, through measures including increasing the use of family group conferencing, where extended family members come together to make decisions about the safe care of children," Ms Bray said.

"Laws which take effect next year mandate the implementation of the Aboriginal child placement principle, which acknowledges connection to country, culture and community as fundamental for the safety, wellbeing and identity of Indigenous children."

Ms Bray said the department had vacancies in Port Lincoln and was actively recruiting to fill them.

"A small number of staff are currently based outside Port Lincoln and regularly travel to the Eyre Peninsula for their roles," she said.

"In many regional areas, fly-in fly-out arrangements are an established workforce model that helps address skill shortages and support the delivery of essential services."

Aboriginal children put in non-Indigenous placements are at risk of losing their sense of identity. (ABC News: James Dunlevie)

Ms Bray said the department offered incentives for staff to move to country locations, including accommodation or subsidised housing, return flights and reimbursement of relocation and education expenses.

She said DCP worked to support children and young people to access health care, with specialist consultants and support teams working alongside staff and carers to connect children with supports tailored to their individual needs.

Children 'criminalised'

Ms Cort said research showed children in care were more likely to end up in the judicial system.

"What we're hearing about the criminalisation of children … confirmed by lived experience, that when children are in out-of-home care, it's more likely that the police will be contacted for small behavioural problems that would normally be privately managed in a home, for example, where police wouldn't intervene," she said.

Generations of families are impacted by a child being put into care, Ms Cort says. (ABC News: James Dunlevie)

"And that intervention starts a pathway that leads to criminalisation, leads to youth justice, and that's confirmed in the research."

She said the placement of a child into care impacted entire generations of families.

"We've also heard of families really grieving the loss of culture that their children experience," Ms Cort said.

Ms Walker said the history of the Stolen Generations was "repeating itself".

"DCP [and] the welfare is more advanced, but it's still the same thing that's happening.

" Our children's identities are being lost, they're disconnected from family, being connected to culture and country. "

Yarning circles have been held at Port Augusta, Port Lincoln and Adelaide. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Yarning circle facilitator Tamara Noel said the carers spoke about feeling unsupported.

"They really wanted DCP and other organisations in the area to come and listen … to hear what their experiences are and to learn from them, to sit with community," Ms Noel said.

Ms Cort said if the solutions could be taken seriously, there was "certainly a light at the end of the tunnel".

title: Major football bodies pen letter seeking Infantino exit over 'deception'
text:
UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC believe FIFA President Gianni Infantino's recent plan to sell an interest in the World Cup was a "fundamental breach of trust" with the institutions world soccer's governing body serves.

In an "open letter to the football family", the governing bodies also said that "when trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned."

UEFA runs football in Europe, CONCACAF does the same for North, Central America and the Caribbean, while the AFC governs the sport in Asia.

FIFA pledges 'full support' for Infantino and apologises for sell-off plan FIFA has reiterated its support for embattled president Gianni Infantino, while apologising to its member associations for the aborted bid to sell off stakes in the World Cup.

The letter was co-signed by UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin, AFC President Salman Bin Ibrahim Al-Khalifa, CONCACAF President Victor Montagliani and three general secretaries.

"Football is the world's greatest shared passion. It belongs to no individual and no institution. It belongs to the players, the fans, the clubs, the member associations and every institution entrusted with safeguarding its future," the open letter said.

"It is in that spirit, as confederations representing its members, that we speak collectively today."

Infantino is facing a revolt after his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private equity investors.

"It is not the conduct of a custodian of the game, but of one who believes the game is answerable to him," the letter said.

"These are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership. That is why we have taken this stance: not lightly and not alone, but together, and out of duty to the game we serve."

Australia's Socceroos also fall under the AFC, which has spoken out against Infantino. (Getty Images: Xinhua/Ziyu Julian Zhu)

UEFA previously issued a threat to boycott the World Cup and other FIFA competitions despite the governing body abandoning and apologising for its failed plan.

Norway's football federation called for Infantino to step down, while the English Football Association has also withdrawn its support for his re-election next March.

"Football's strength has always been its unity. We call for that unity to be honoured now," the letter said. "For leadership that serves football, not seeks to command it."

Last Wednesday, FIFA said it had apologised for errors made over the failed plan but that senior staff at a crisis meeting in Morocco "reaffirmed their full support" for his presidency.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

However, the nature of the meeting was also met with criticism.

"FIFA's own letter also confirms that only one elected official was present at the leadership meeting in Morocco," the open letter said.

"No FIFA Council members or Member Associations were invited to participate. Only the management committee, composed of FIFA-employed senior staff, was present."

FIFA was also urged to go further than just acknowledging mistakes were made.

"It treats this as a failure of communication, when what football witnessed was a failure of judgement," the letter said.

"There remains no recognition that attempting to sell an interest in the FIFA World Cup was a profound failure of judgement — not just a procedural misstep, but a fundamental breach of trust with the very institutions FIFA exists to serve."

In a statement Saturday, FIFA defended Infantino against what it called a "concerted and ongoing effort" to undermine his leadership of the organisation.

That statement followed a report by British newspaper The Daily Telegraph raising questions about an exit package paid by UEFA to a female staffer who worked with Infantino when he was general secretary of European soccer's ruling body.

UEFA confirmed a "departure payment" was made to the employee and said it was "in line" with regulations at the time.

Infantino worked at UEFA for 16 years before being elected FIFA president.

AP

title: Charles Darwin University to be bound to KPIs by government after scandals
text:
The Northern Territory's only university will soon face strict new guidelines for how it is allowed to spend government funds, following a series of bungles and the failure of an overseas campus.

Charles Darwin University (CDU) has lurched from one crisis to the next during the past 12 months, from a TAFE accreditation blunder, to $4 million owed in staff underpayments.

In February, CDU also scrapped plans to open a London campus, after spending nearly $2 million on the initiative despite the university having no enrolled students in the UK.

CDU's vice-chancellor Scott Bowman stepped down during the scandals in February.

Jo Hersey says if CDU does not meet its KPIs, "I will look to divert resources to other training providers". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Today, NT Education Minister Jo Hersey said the government would overhaul its partnership with CDU and require it to abide by new key performance indicators (KPIs).

"I am bringing forward these changes to end the frustration and unnecessary costs in time and money students and their families have been caught up in," she said in a statement.

"We must have accountability for Territorians' money invested into our training providers to make sure that we maximise outcomes.

"In order to grow the economy, we need strong training providers to give Territorians the best training for their chosen pathways, and we will use the renegotiating of a new agreement to build a strong relationship with CDU."

An NT government spokesperson said its 2026-27 budget allocation to CDU was $61.4 million.

CDU's Danala campus, in the Darwin CBD, opened in 2024 after securing a $151 million loan from the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

'Work has begun' on law changes

Mrs Hersey cited the TAFE scandal, as well as a further bungle this year which saw around 100 CDU students miss out on their electro-technology training, as reasons behind her decision to take action.

"The new agreement will have KPIs for outcomes, rather than untied funding without KPIs," she said.

"If KPIs are not met I will look to divert resources to other training providers — it's just too critical that we get this right.

"Work on legislative amendments has begun and I will work with the sector with a view to it being introduced into NT Parliament in early 2027."

Charles Darwin University vice-chancellor resigns Charles Darwin University's vice-chancellor Scott Bowman has resigned following an accreditation scandal that has impacted almost 300 of the university's TAFE students.

In recent years, CDU also secured a $151 million loan from the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility and broad government support to build a brand new campus in the Darwin CBD.

As well as that Danala campus and its other Darwin facilities, CDU has campuses in Palmerston, Katherine, Alice Springs, Sydney and other interstate locations.

The law changes will also include the Batchelor Institute of Indigenous Tertiary Education, which has also faced scrutiny in recent years over financial anomalies and governance flaws.

CDU says it remains focused on students

In a statement, a CDU spokesperson said the university recognised "the importance of strong governance and accountability and will work constructively with the NT government on proposed legislative changes and the development of a new partnership agreement".

"CDU is committed to providing high-quality education and training that meets the needs of Territorians, as it has done for more than 30 years," they said.

"CDU is already acting following a recent internal review into competency issues to strengthen its vocational education and training operations to ensure students receive the training and support they need to successfully complete their qualifications."

The spokesperson also said the university's focus remained "firmly on its students and ensuring they graduate with the skills, knowledge and capabilities needed to succeed in the workforce and contribute to the Territory's future".

title: US guru who analyses music turns his focus to Sydney teen's debut single
text:
His musical analysis videos have attracted billions of views on YouTube. Now influential US musician and producer Rick Beato has heaped praise on the debut single by 13-year-old Sydney performer Niko Karolia.

Beato has more than 5.7 million subscribers and 2.06 billion views on his YouTube channel, where he breaks down songs and interviews legendary musicians.

His large and growing audience has helped him land interviews with some of the biggest names in music, like Queen's Brian May, Sting, Pink Floyd's David Gilmour and recently Billy Joel.

Sting is among the high-profile musicians who have appeared on Rick Beato's YouTube show. (YouTube: Rick Beato)

Beato will be in Australia in October for a series of live shows, with his Sydney date upgraded to a bigger venue to meet demand.

The shows will include a live version of his popular What Makes This Song Great? segment, in which he takes a deep dive into the songwriting, production and musical techniques behind well-known songs.

Songs analysed on his channel include Elton John's Tiny Dancer, Coldplay's The Scientist, Fleetwood Mac's Go Your Own Way and Nirvana's Smells Like Teen Spirit.

Breaking down Sana

During an interview with Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings, Beato was asked to analyse Sana, the debut single from Karolia, who recently made her first-ever radio appearance on the program.

"I mean, it's really putting you on the spot, but can you dissect that for us?" Macdonald asked.

Beato was impressed by the soulful track, highlighting the strength of Karolia's songwriting.

"Very strong melody that has a natural 'da da, da da,'" he said, humming a musical phrase to conclude his sentence.

"It has a natural resolution to it, like within it.

"Take away the chords, take away the arrangement around it, the melody is strong enough on its own to be sung with no accompaniment, which is really what you want to have.

"As soon as I start listening to a melody like that, those are the things I listen for."

Rick Beato says Niko Karolia's debut single Sana has a "very strong melody". (Supplied)

Beato also identified a songwriting technique used in the song, that is employed in nursery rhymes such as Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star.

It is known as antecedent and consequent, where one phrase asks a musical question, and the next answers it.

"Strong melodies will have those things," Beato said.

"And in the sections I just listened to, they have melodies that are written like that, that are very strong."

'I just want to be a global pop star'

Karolia told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings she wants to take on the world.

"I just want to be a global pop star that people can resonate with," she said.

"At the start of last year, this idea popped into my head that I wanted to start releasing music."

The 13-year-old was joined by her father, Imz Karolia, during the interview.

Niko Karolia says the idea to start releasing music popped into her head last year. (Instagram: @nikokarolia)

He was initially hesitant about his daughter launching a music career, but changed his mind when he saw the effort she was putting in.

"There were arguments," she said.

" I was just trying to prove to him that I can release music, and I am ready to release music. "

Mr Karolia said his daughter's musical and performing talent had been apparent from an early age.

"Oh yeah, man. From the time she was a baby," he said.

"I've got videos of her dancing and singing and playing around when she was like six months old."

He said they enrolled her in performing arts programs when she was about four years old.

"It's my job as a father to really understand what natural talent my kids have and cultivate that for them, open the right doors for them," he said.

Karolia writes her own songs, collaborating with several people, including fellow performers Tanisha and Jess Jade, and her cousin Jake Sta-Maria and her father.
