Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met with Vietnamese President To Lam in Canberra today and lauded Australia’s relationship with the country as a critical pillar of his government’s commitment to maintaining and strengthening relations in South-East Asia.

During the talks, Vietnam agreed to the removal of trade barriers for the export of Australian kangaroo and deer meat, which will enable its open market access to the goods.

Vietnamese President To Lam (centre) and his delegation during their meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen

In a joint statement released by the pair after their meeting, Albanese said the two countries had agreed to “stronger co-operation across defence, maritime and border security, the digital economy, agriculture, energy, minerals, science and innovation”.

It is Lam’s first state visit to Australia since his appointment as president in 2024.

title: Sarah Pound’s slow-cooker Moroccan vegetable and chickpea stew
text:
Step 1 Place a large frying pan over medium-high heat and add the olive oil. Add the onion and cook for 4-5 minutes until softened.

Step 2 Add the garlic and Moroccan seasoning and cook for another minute until fragrant. If the pan starts catching on the bottom slightly, add a splash of vegetable stock or water to help lift the flavour.

Step 3 Stir through the harissa paste and sweet potato and cook for 2-3 minutes, coating the vegetables in the spices.

Step 4 Transfer the contents of the pan to the slow cooker. Add the chickpeas, cauliflower, capsicum, tomato paste, diced tomato, vegetable stock, apricots and honey. Mix well.

Step 5 Place the lid on and cook on high for 3 hours. Then add the zucchini and stir through gently. Continue cooking for another hour until all the vegetables are tender and the stew has thickened slightly.

title: Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again
text:
Advertisement

BusinessBanking & financeFederal Reserve Opinion Meddler-in-chief: Trump is up to his old tricks again Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 11, 2026 — 11:55am

August 11, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Even with his handpicked man in the chair of the Federal Reserve Board, Donald Trump can’t help himself. He is still trying to gain more influence, even control, of the US central bank and its decision-making. Last week, he renewed efforts to sack Fed governor Lisa Cook that were thwarted earlier this year by the US Supreme Court, reviving an untested allegation that she had committed mortgage fraud prior to her appointment to the Fed’s board of governors in 2023. Kevin Warsh has been at pains to try to distance himself from any suggestion that he is a “sock puppet” for Trump, presenting himself as an inflation hawk, ready to raise rates if required. Aresna Villaneuva The Supreme Court, while not offering an opinion on the allegations against her, had left Cook in place while litigation to remove her continued, saying that Trump had failed to give her proper notice or an opportunity to respond to the allegations. A Fed governor can only be removed “for cause,” which is generally thought to mean serious wrongdoing or malfeasance while in office.

Advertisement

Trump has now revived his attempt to oust her from the board and open a vacancy that he could fill with someone more amenable to his desire for lower US interest rates. The White House has served her with a letter giving notice that Trump was considering removing her from the board “due to there being sufficient reason to believe that you made false statements on one or more mortgage agreements”. The letter said that “even if your conduct does not rise to the level of a felony offence, it appears to demonstrate a level of gross negligence in financial transactions that calls into question your competence and trustworthiness as a financial regulator.” Related Article Opinion

Japan Why fears of a Japanese implosion have the world on edge Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Her actions, it said, “may be sufficient to demonstrate that you committed a crime, as you appear to have acquired mortgages that do not meet certain lending requirements and could have received favourable loan terms under fraudulent circumstances. “Based on these facts, a jury could find that you intended to defraud these institutions for your own benefit, but at a minimum, this conduct was grossly negligent and demonstrates that you are unfit for the office in which you serve as a controlling member of the Federal Reserve.”

Advertisement

The allegation against Cook, brought forward by Trump loyalist Bill Pulte, the former director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, is that she misled her lender by claiming two separate properties as her principal place of residence in order to gain a lower interest rate. Cook, however, has referred to a clerical error in the documentation, and there have been a number of reports from those who have seen the loan documents that say that her application for the loans makes it clear that the second property was a holiday or second home and therefore the lender should have been aware that it wasn’t her principal place of residence. Donald Trump has renewed his push to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook. Bloomberg Trump, of course, isn’t concerned about the facts or due process – his original attempt to fire Cook came via a social media post – but remains committed to trying to stack the Fed board with loyalists who will deliver him the lower rates he has long obsessed about. He failed to force former Fed chair, Jerome Powell – whom he threatened with criminal charges over over-runs in the cost of renovating the Fed’s Washington headquarters – to vacate his position.

Advertisement

Indeed, that effort backfired, with Powell breaking the convention that retiring Fed chairs leave the board, vowing to remain until it was certain that the charges wouldn’t be revived. His term doesn’t expire until January 2028. Related Article Opinion

Federal Reserve Trump will be furious as an old foe digs in his heels Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Cook, whose 14-year term is scheduled to end in 2038, is also not going to go quietly, with her lawyers describing the allegation “as baseless now as they were a year ago when President Trump tried to remove Governor Cook and interfere with the independence of the Federal Reserve.” She has vowed to continue fighting the allegations, which haven’t been tested in a court because no formal charges have been laid. To date, the court actions have been about process – whether Trump has the power to unilaterally fire her – not the underlying allegations. The issue at stake, as it was with Trump’s attempts to remove Powell, with whom he had a testy relationship because Powell wouldn’t do his bidding, isn’t so much the individual fate of Cook, but what it could mean for the independence of the Fed.

Advertisement

There is plenty of research that says the independence of a central bank from its government is correlated with lower inflation rates. Politicians want pro-cyclical monetary policies and lower interest rates to boost growth. Central bankers generally tend towards counter-cyclical policies to control inflation. The inflation-fighting credibility of the central bank has a significant influence over market interest rates – the bond yields that actually help determine the rates businesses and consumers pay. Financial markets have shown they still have their doubts on Warsh. Bloomberg That’s why Fed chairs and officials try to keep their relationships with presidents and other political figures at arms-length, although it has been normal for Fed chairs to meet regularly, even weekly, with the US Treasury secretary and other senior economic officials. Warsh has been at pains to try to distance himself from any suggestion that he is a “sock puppet” for Trump, presenting himself as an inflation hawk, ready to raise rates if required.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump’s great humiliation: Middle East may be entering a post-American era Peter Hartcher Political and international editor Financial market participants have yet to be completely convinced that Warsh will be as hawkish on inflation as he presents and recent revelations that Trump speaks frequently with him have added to their unease. Trump’s National Economic Council director, Kevin Hassett, told Bloomberg last Friday that Trump and Warsh “talk about the economy all the time, although he was “sure” the president didn’t pressure Warsh on interest rate decisions and respected the independence of the Fed. Trump himself claimed that he had spoken to Warsh “one time briefly” a few days ago: “just a conversation.” “They (the reports) made it sound like I live and breathe, you know, I speak to Kevin all the time, every time,” he said.

Advertisement

As if the rates-obsessed Trump wouldn’t raise the topic of interest rates with the Fed, who he believes would cut rates if only the other 11 members of the committee that sets US monetary policy weren’t “political” and determined “to keep rates up.” Trump, of course, isn’t concerned about the facts or due process – his original attempt to fire Cook came via a social media post – but remains committed to trying to stack the Fed board with loyalists who will deliver him the lower rates he has long obsessed about. Trump doesn’t appear to have grasped that, while the Fed might be able to anchor the short end of the yield curve, the market sets the longer-term yields/rates that matter to the economy. When the Fed left its policy rate unchanged at last month’s meeting, and Warsh failed to provide guidance and made some comments interpreted as being “dovish,” the yields on longer-duration bonds spiked immediately. Trump might not be concerned about a US inflation rate that has been elevated by his tax cuts, trade wars and the war in the Middle East, but by investors holding bonds that might mature in 10 years, or 30 years’ time are.

Advertisement

This week’s consumer price index is expected to reflect a slight easing in inflation in July (because it covers a period when there was a ceasefire in the Middle East) but, with no end to the war in sight, higher oil, gasoline and diesel prices are likely to seep more widely into the economy and flow through to an inflation rate that has been well above the Fed’s 2 per cent target for more than five years. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America Fool’s gold: Trump is set to break his promise to America Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The continuing pursuit of Cook and the apparent closeness of the relationship between Trump and Warsh means that the question mark over the Fed’s continuing independence will remain. Bond traders talk about a risk premium having been added to bond yields to reflect Warsh’s withdrawal of forward guidance from his and the Fed’s commentary and the uncertainty over his inflation-fighting credentials. If Trump continues to try to unseat Cook, and keeps Warsh on speed dial, they might well add another layer of premium to those yields. title: She’s the world’s best female swimmer. And she wants Ariarne Titmus’ world record
text:
Advertisement

SportSwimmingSwimming She’s the world’s best female swimmer. And she wants Ariarne Titmus’ world record Tom Decent August 11, 2026 — 11:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Irvine, California: Swimming superstar Summer McIntosh says she’s out to break the 200m freestyle world record held by Australia’s Ariarne Titmus at this week’s Pan Pacific Championships in California, a feat that would put the Canadian alongside Australian legend Shane Gould in the record books. The world’s best female swimmer, who claimed three individual gold medals at the 2024 Paris Olympics, arrives in Irvine as the star attraction ahead of four days of racing, starting on Wednesday (Thursday morning AEST), against the best swimmers from Australia, the United States and other non-European nations. Ariarne Titmus (centre) after winning gold in the women’s 400m freestyle at the 2024 Paris Olympics ahead of Summer McIntosh (left) and Katie Ledecky (right). Getty Images While Australia will be without several of its biggest names, including Mollie O’Callaghan, Kaylee McKeown and Cam McEvoy, McIntosh skipped the recent Commonwealth Games to ensure she was peaking for the Pan Pacs, which haven’t been held since 2018. The 19-year-old won’t contest the 800m freestyle against Australia’s Lani Pallister and US great Katie Ledecky, but has entered five events in Irvine: the 200m freestyle, 400m freestyle, 200m butterfly and both individual medleys.

Advertisement

McIntosh owns the world record in every event she is racing this week except the 200m freestyle, which belongs to Titmus after her narrow victory over O’Callaghan in a time of 1:52.23 at Australia’s Olympic trials in 2024. It is an event McIntosh has pushed down her list of priorities in recent years. She took bronze behind O’Callaghan and Titmus at the 2023 world championships in 1:53.65 – which remains her personal best – but did not contest it at the Paris Olympics or last year’s world championships due to a large program. Canadian swim sensation Summer McIntosh. Getty Images With Titmus retired and O’Callaghan nursing a back issue, McIntosh is eager to make an early statement in Irvine, with finals on day one starting at midday AEST (Thursday). “Day one for the 200m freestyle I think I will be the most hyped up for because I haven’t raced that internationally in a long time,” McIntosh said. “I think that will be the most interesting. Day one will be a great way to start off the meet.

Advertisement

“I’m always trying to go to best times, whether that’s a world record that I already have or a world record that I don’t have. The 200m freestyle world record is probably one of the toughest world records in the books. “Seeing Josh [Liendo] and Kylie [Masse] and all those [Canadian] guys do their thing [at Commonwealth Games] definitely got me hyped up and motivated heading into Pan Pacs. I’m feeling really good heading into this competition.” Swimming world records held by Summer McIntosh (longcourse) 200m butterfly: 2:01.65 — Montreal, Canada, July 2026

2:01.65 — Montreal, Canada, July 2026 400m freestyle: 3:54.18 — Victoria, Canada, June 2025

3:54.18 — Victoria, Canada, June 2025 200m individual medley: 2:05.70 — Victoria, Canada, June 2025

2:05.70 — Victoria, Canada, June 2025 400m individual medley: 4:23.65 — Victoria, Canada, June 2025 O’Callaghan is the reigning Olympic and world champion in the 200m freestyle but faces a battle to retain her supremacy now McIntosh is turning her attention back to the event. Asked about O’Callaghan’s absence, McIntosh said: “It’s very tough to see that she’s injured and that sucks. I’m sure she’s very frustrated. I hope she makes a speedy recovery. She’s an amazing athlete … and I’m excited for when she gets back.”

Advertisement

Titmus beat McIntosh in the 400m freestyle final at the Paris Olympics two years but lost her world record in the event to the Canadian last year. If McIntosh can break Titmus’ 200m mark on Wednesday (Thursday AEST), she will hold five individual longcourse world records simultaneously. Shane Gould after the 1972 Olympics. Fairfax Media Gould, Kornelia Ender and Michael Phelps are the only other swimmers to have managed such a feat. In 1972, Gould held every women’s freestyle world record from 100m to 1500m at the same time. McIntosh is now trained by Bob Bowman, who coached Phelps to become the most decorated Olympian in history and also oversees French great Leon Marchand. Bowman has already drawn comparisons between McIntosh and Phelps.

Advertisement

“Hearing that is very flattering,” McIntosh said of the comparisons. “Michael Phelps is the greatest swimmer of all time and definitely my idol. Hearing [Bowman] even remotely compare us is pretty crazy and very flattering. I take great pride in that. Related Article Swimming ‘Smash those Yanks’: Short channels Gary Hall jnr and doubles down on US sledge “We go fast every single day. There are no days off with him. There’s no recovery practices.” McIntosh’s program for the Los Angeles Olympics in two years has already become a source of great intrigue in the swimming world, particularly because the 200m butterfly and 800m freestyle clash on the final day of competition. However, Pallister can breathe a sigh of relief, with McIntosh admitting it was unlikely she would contest the 800m freestyle in LA – an event in which Ledecky will be chasing an extraordinary fifth consecutive Olympic gold medal.

“There’s lots of options. There’s six or seven events I could do. I’m keeping it open right now,” McIntosh said. “Most likely no [for the 800m freestyle]. The 200 fly is that day, so that’s my favourite event and I’ll be doing that. “[On the flight to the USA] I hadn’t opened the window during the whole plane ride. As we’re about to land, I see SoFi Stadium and I got full-body chills just imaging two years from now where I am going to be. title: Australia confront Cameron Green question ahead of Darwin Test
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia confront Cameron Green question ahead of Darwin Test Daniel Brettig August 11, 2026 — 11:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cameron Green spent 30 minutes locked in earnest conversation with captain Pat Cummins and coach Andrew McDonald at training on Tuesday morning as the trio wrestled with the biggest question in Australian cricket. How does the team find a way to get the best out of 27-year-old Green, who after six summers in a baggy green is yet to fully capitalise on his outrageous talent. All-rounder Cameron Green (centre) signing autographs for cricket fans in Darwin flanked by Beau Webster (left) and Steve Smith. Getty Images While there are no suggestions that Green will be dropped from the team this week – certainly not judging by the movements of reserve batter Josh Inglis – it is no secret that the West Australian all-rounder has been close to the edge of selection in recent times. There have also been concerns that, despite having been in and around the team for six years, he is yet to find a settled place within it, both on and off the field.

Advertisement

Australian captain Pat Cummins, all-rounder Cameron green and coach Andrew McDonald in deep conversations in darwin as the team prepares for the first Test against Bangladesh. Daniel Brettig There is a marked contrast between Green and the older, more streetwise Beau Webster, who was never identified as a long-term Test player in the same way as Green but has shown with plenty of grit and cricket smarts that he is capable of holding his own at international level. “The biggest thing I’ve learned is that I’m good enough at this level,” Webster said as Green, Cummins and McDonald did their conversational laps of the oval. “You never really know. “The question in the lead-up to that first Test was, ‘do you feel ready’, and although I was bluffing myself saying ‘absolutely’, at the end of the day you don’t really know until you get out there and face the bowlers from other countries and are put into situations with big crowds and big moments in games of cricket where you’re expected to perform. That was the biggest tick over the last 12 months. “I forced my way into this team through weight of runs ... primarily as a batter you deal in runs, and that’s been my way into the team and the way to stay in the team. What I’ve done in my first eight Tests with the bat has probably showed I can be considered a genuine top-six batter.”

Advertisement

Green's best has been outstanding. There was a match-winning century in Wellington against New Zealand on a tough pitch in 2024, another hundred in India the year before, and some superb catches and bowling spells along the way. But last summer during an Ashes series largely dominated by Australia, Green struggled to find his best, summed up when he was bowled by a Yorker he could barely reach after backing away in anticipation of a short ball under lights at the Gabba. Spinner Nathan Lyon shares a laugh with cricket fans in Darwin ahead of the Test match starting Thursday. Getty Images There have also been other moments, whether a confrontation with a journalist at a Sheffield Shield game or an on-field protest about the bowling action of Pakistan's Usman Tariq (for which he later apologised), that have raised the question of whether he is concentrating on the right things. Webster, for his part, has been consistent in his belief that the two all-rounders can co-exist in the team.

Advertisement

“I don’t see why not,” Webster said. “It’s surely more of a benefit to have more options in that top seven with the ball, and I certainly don’t see it as a direct competition. It only adds more option and more benefits for the captain if we’re both performing with the bat, with both of our main skill, and what we can offer in the field. Related Article Australian cricket ‘I haven’t done enough’: Weatherald admits he could be dropped without top end runs “I love playing with Cameron, I love having the options if he’s on with the ball or if I’m on with the ball, we can chop and change if the big three and the spinner need a chop-out. So I’m more than happy. “I’m just happy doing my job and making myself hard to leave out of the 11, whether that’s with the bat or the ball. I pride myself on being able to contribute in all facets of the game, and so does he. It just so happens that we’re allrounders and both primarily batters.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

title: ‘He thought it was funny’: Emails from fake staffer ‘Jessica’ exposed at ICAC
text:
Advertisement

A lobbyist being investigated by the state’s corruption watchdog says invoices sent under a fake name were just “silly humour” and not part of an elaborate scheme to hide illegal donations. Jeremy Greenwood also told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Tuesday he had a phone call earlier that morning with another key person of interest in the Operation Rosny inquiry, Christian Ellis, but struggled to recall details of the exchange. Jeremy Greenwood arrives at the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Tuesday. Peter Rae The ICAC is investigating several allegations against Greenwood, including that he agreed to share in a $2 million bribe from fugitive developer Jean Nassif, and that his company Beckington was used to wash funds from Catholic Schools NSW to support the work of a conservative sub-faction known as the Reformers. Asked about an invoice sent from Beckington to Catholic Schools NSW in 2020, the lobbyist and one-time political operative conceded the person who sent the email, “Jessica”, was a fake name made up by his business partner Christian Ellis.

Advertisement

“He just thought it was funny,” Greenwood said. Counsel assisting the commission, Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, replied: “I’m not getting the joke.” Greenwood then explained he and Ellis had “silly humour, sorry”. Catholic schools funding in spotlight Payments from Catholic Schools NSW to Greenwood’s two companies, Beckington and JPG Advisory, form a central plank of the ICAC’s claim that sham invoices were used to support the Reformers’ work in stacking branches across Sydney.

Advertisement

Catholic Schools NSW ultimately paid Beckington $130,900 over two years. Related Article Live

Operation Rosny ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Jeremy Greenwood pressed on Beckington’s payments from Catholic Schools NSW, 6am phone call with Christian Ellis “The commission has found no evidence of services being undertaken by Beckington for Catholic Schools NSW between August 2019 and August 2021,” Dwyer said. Greenwood responded: “A lot of work was done verbally, in person in the office. I just can’t recall it. I know it was happening.” Catholic Schools NSW chief executive and fellow Reformer Dallas McInerney is due to give evidence at the ICAC on Wednesday and Thursday.

Advertisement

Greenwood was also pressed on how much money Beckington paid to Jean-Claude Perrottet to cover him for doing Reformers work. Greenwood said he had given some money to the younger brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet but could not recall why, how much, or when. Dwyer then asked Greenwood if he discussed his evidence with anyone overnight, including the issue of payments to Jean-Claude. He revealed Ellis, Greenwood’s Beckington business partner who moved to the United Kingdom this year, called him about 6am on Tuesday on the encrypted app Signal. Ellis, according to Greenwood, wanted to know the commission’s reaction to Greenwood revealing that his overseas-based mate would be prepared to provide evidence to the commission. Greenwood told Ellis that it was “noted” by the commission. He said he could not remember much about the phone call, even though it had occurred less than five hours earlier.

Advertisement

The ICAC has previously said Ellis has declined to assist its inquiry. $1000 payments in doubt On Monday, Greenwood told the commission that Reformer and fellow Liberal operative Jean-Claude Perrottet had received “$1000 payments” to answer Greenwood’s phone while he was overseas for three weeks. ICAC counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, Juliet Curtin and Hugo Wilesmith enter the corruption watchdog’s building on Tuesday. Peter Rae Greenwood said given the timezone differences, he did not want to be woken up by calls from Australia nor did he want clients to hear the international dialtone when trying to contact him.

Advertisement

Dwyer returned to the issue on Tuesday, stating to Greenwood: “Aren’t you just making that up now to try and justify why you said that you were paying Jean-Claude Perrottet money to divert the phones?” Greenwood responded: “I am not making anything up in this process.” The inquiry continues.

title: I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaMental health Opinion I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate Updated August 11, 2026 — 11:34am , first published 11:30am

Updated August 11, 2026 — 11:34am ,first published 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The reform of mental health care is elusive and tantalising. In my 40 plus years in psychiatry, I have seen the system repeatedly cycle between scandal and the promise of a new era. Hope and optimism flatter to deceive, and what feels like a tipping point always turns out to be a mirage. In a triumph of hope over experience, I really thought that the landmark Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System would break this cycle. However, this has turned out not only to be a mirage, but another false dawn. Professor Patrick McGorry served as chair of the expert advisory committee of the Royal Commission into the Victorian Mental Health System. The royal commission was necessary because of the collapse of the public mental health system which, after the ultimately reckless closure of the standalone mental hospitals, had been downsized and absorbed into general hospitals in the 1990s and neglected ever since.

Advertisement

The Victorian government was the first – and so far only – state government to own this policy failure, admitting the system was “broken” and establishing a royal commission in 2018. The commission’s expert advisory committee, which I had the privilege to chair, produced a carefully formulated and sequenced blueprint with 74 transformational recommendations. At that time, the political will and community support was unprecedented. There was bipartisan support and a historic joint sitting of the parliament launched the final report. It seemed that the fair go that people with mental illness and so many dedicated colleagues had dreamed about would finally be realised. The early signs were promising. Mental health was committed to as a signature reform, powered by a groundbreaking new levy to future-proof the rebuild, anticipating looming financial challenges. The then-deputy premier James Merlino took on the role of minister for mental health. Regional mental health boards were established to independently commission services, and an independent Mental Health Commission was set up by the government as a statutory authority to keep itself and future governments honest – and to safeguard the reform.

Advertisement

Over the past three years, whatever momentum there once was has now evaporated. We have seen a revolving door of ministers, with the issue being marginalised and now buried within the main Health portfolio. The Victorian Department of Health, which assumed a much more powerful role, made the fatal mistake of entrusting departmental officials who lacked crucial experience of mental health care and system reform, and who have been stubbornly immune to advice from experts. The mental health levy raises more than $1 billion a year from the business sector. But with major budget pressures afflicting the government, many in the sector believe this funding is being diverted to prop up the broader hospital system and state finances. If true, this would represent a major breach of faith. In 2017, I delivered the Redmond Barry Public Lecture at the State Library with the title “Victoria’s Mental Breakdown”. This speech helped to create momentum for the royal commission. Almost a decade on, Victoria still hasn’t recovered from the breakdown. Today, the culture and quality of mental health services are worse.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Psychology I was recruited into a cult as a teenager. Here’s how it happened Ahona Guha Psychologist The ambulances are still all at the bottom of the cliff. Acute units remain custodial and

non-therapeutic. Clinical research, a cornerstone of health care, is an endangered species, and in contrast to the rest of health care, few if any of recent treatment advances are available to patients. The core system is not a priority. The risks to patients, to staff through both moral and physical injury, and to the wider community have continued to worsen as the workforce wilts and

demand surges. This is the worst kept secret in Victoria and a once-in-a-generation opportunity has so far been squandered. It is a classic case of implementation failure, which no amount of spin can conceal. Yet for the past three years, the government has claimed progress is being made in line with the spirit and recommendations of the royal commission.

Advertisement

This gaslights not only people and families of their own experiences, but also frontline clinicians and their leadership, who are denied the right to speak publicly. Related Article Opinion

Real life I worked at Lifeline. There’s a reason why people repeat themselves Alison Fonseca Journalist Further evidence of bad faith over the past two years is the undermining of watchdog and accountability mechanisms – notably the scrapping of the regional boards, which were to commission mental health services, the sidelining of lived experience, the shrinkage and weakening of the Mental Health Commission, and the dramatic reduction in funding for the peak body, Mental Health Victoria. The end result is that people with severe mental illnesses remain banished to the margins of society, consigned to languish in their bedrooms, or suffer on the streets or in jail. But the mirage can be transcended with solutions.

Advertisement

Mental health care desperately needs government failures to be acknowledged, and a new direction. As the state election looms, Victorians deserve to know that mental health is a top priority that both sides of politics are committed to reforming. Patrick McGorry is a professor youth mental health and the University of Melbourne and served as chair of the expert advisory committee of the Royal Commission into the Victorian Mental Health System. title: Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Work-from-home law delayed by Carroll weeks before planned start Angus Delaney August 11, 2026 — 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians will not have a legal right to work from home until at least July next year, after Labor delayed its plan to introduce the controversial law following an eleventh-hour plea from business groups. Premier Ben Carroll announced on Tuesday that as part of his government’s “reset with the business community”, the law would not come into effect until July 1, 2027, 10 months after the original intended September start date. Premier Ben Carroll, pictured last month, has delayed Labor’s work-from-home legislation. Justin McManus “I support work from home. I support flexible work. It is good for working families,” Carroll said. But he said the state’s economic health was important, and he wanted business to thrive in Victoria. “That is why I’ve delayed these changes,” he said.

Advertisement

Related Article Victorian election Pay for the desk or pay a penalty: Inside Victoria’s strict new work-from-home rules The bill was expected to pass parliament’s upper house on Thursday, but the government will now delay its passage, although Carroll promised it would still pass before the November state election. He said he would consult on any “commonsense amendments”. The move to delay the legislation has been welcomed by industry and business groups, which on Monday joined forces to call for the bill to be scrapped, and warned that it risked increasing unemployment and driving investment out of the state. Tim Piper, Victorian head of the Australian Industry Group, said businesses were still concerned the legislation was going ahead at all, but there was now at least opportunity for the government to consider amendments and improvements.

Advertisement

Piper said the government should use the delay to consider scrapping the bill entirely and conduct an economic impact statement on the potential fallout. “When you have an economic impact statement, you can understand whether there’s likely to be a detrimental, whether it’s like whether it’s likely to be detrimental or not. We think it is,” Piper said. Labor’s promise to legislate a right to work from home two days a week has angered business groups, which say it will send jobs and investment interstate. Getty Images The concession from Labor is a sign Carroll is following through on his commitment to be a more pro-business premier than predecessor Jacinta Allan. The business lobby will still push Labor to ditch the policy altogether, though the government and opposition have reaffirmed their support for employees’ work-from-home rights.

Advertisement

Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain said the decision to pause the debate over the “divisive legislation” and listen to industry was a good start, but maintained the bill should be scrapped. Related Article Victorian Parliament Coalition to support working-from-home laws but want changes to protect businesses “The premier has been in touch with us directly and indicated he is willing to meet with us,” Curtain said in a statement. “We hope to persuade him to abandon this destructive course.”



Bran Black, chief executive of the Business Council of Australia, said while Carroll was taking “the first steps towards” listening to industry, the bill in any form would “compound Victoria’s economic decline”. “Already, Victoria has the highest unemployment rate in the country and the Victorian economy cannot afford another policy that drives investment and jobs away, which only hurts Victorians through lower living standards,” Black said. Cath Evans, Victorian executive director of the Property Council, said the delay would allow businesses to work with government on introducing amendments.

“The delay is welcome, but this is not the end of the process,” Evans said. The Coalition under Opposition Leader Jess Wilson decided not to oppose Labor’s bill and was seeking to introduce amendments to protect businesses. The proposed amendments include capping “reasonable costs” an employer must pay at $1000, limiting the right to employees who primarily work in Victoria and will continue to do so (unless mutually agreed to), and delaying an employee’s right to appeal a company’s decision until next year. Shadow Attorney-General James Newbury said Carroll had broken a promise to Victorians by pushing the start date back 10 months. “Ben Carroll has proven that he cannot be trusted. His Government made a guarantee that these laws would be in place on 1 September, a guarantee he has broken. Victorians cannot trust this Premier or his Labor Government.”

Major business groups on Monday warned the proposed overhaul was another layer of red tape that would result in companies deserting Victoria and expanding their businesses interstate. Business groups have not ruled out launching or joining a potential High Court challenge against the legislation if it passes. Legal experts have cast doubt over the state government’s ability to legislate a right to work from home, as most workplace laws are under the jurisdiction of the federal government. The Australian sharemarket edged higher in early trade as energy stocks rallied due the latest jump in oil prices amid the US-Iranian stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz, as investors awaited the interest rate decision by the Reserve Bank this afternoon. The local bourse slid 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.58¢. Wall Street has kicked off its week with a slightly weaker session. AP The Reserve Bank announces its interest rates decision at 2.30pm AEST, with money markets and economists in near-unanimous agreement that the central bank’s monetary policy board will hold the cash rate steady at 4.35 per cent when it wraps up its latest two-day meeting. Southern Cross Media, the business created from the merger of Kerry Stokes’ Seven West and radio group Southern Cross, dropped 1.8 per cent after announcing a $13 million loss for the 2025 financial year due to deteriorating market conditions. The group, which owns the Seven Network, The West Australian newspaper and Triple M network, said revenue dropped across television, newspapers and radio. Kerry Stokes’ SGH, which owns 20.1 per cent of Southern Cross Media, slumped 8.3 per cent after saying its net profit stalled at $920 million. Related Article Updated

While its revenues in the June quarter jumped 38 per cent to $US159 million ($225.4 million), its operating expenses grew by 43 per cent, helping push quarterly net profit down to $US5.1 million, from $US7 million a year ago. The fall overshadowed gains by software makers WiseTech Global (up 0.8 per cent) and Xero (up 1.3 per cent). Meanwhile, oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos jumped 3 per cent and 4.1 per cent, respectively, as oil prices climbed again overnight amid dimming hopes for a breakthrough in the standoff between the United States and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that normally carries as much as one-fifth of the world’s oil supply. The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil, climbed nearly 5 per cent to about $US88 a barrel, trading 16 per cent higher now than before the start of the war. West Texas Intermediate crude, the US benchmark, also moved higher by 5 per cent, to $82 a barrel.

Iran and Oman recently indicated that they were near an agreement that would allow oil and other important commercial traffic to resume through the crucial waterway. But Iran has issued a long list of demands that it said would have to be met by the US before ships could move freely again, including reparations payments for the war. US President Donald Trump in turn demanded compensation from Iran for all the people they have killed in conflicts after Tehran. Trump said in a social media post that he will put the new demands “firmly into any, and all, future negotiations.” The hardening stance makes it unlikely that Tehran and Washington will be able to agree to any immediate pact to end the war and ease the strain on global energy supplies. The ongoing uncertainty also benefited local refiners Ampol and Viva Energy, which gained 2.1 per cent and 2.5 per cent, while coal producers Yancoal and Whitehaven rose 2.8 per cent and 3.1 per cent, respectively, amid bets the oil crunch will bolster demand for their fossil fuel. Mining stocks were also higher in early trade, with BHP up 1.3 per cent, Rio Tinto up 0.5 per cent and Fortescue up 1.1 per cent. Gold miners Northern Star added 0.9 per cent and Evolution Mining gained 2 per cent as bullion prices rose to nearly $US4400 an ounce. On the flipside, shares of companies with high fuel dependency such as airlines declined. Qantas fell 2.4 per cent, and Virgin Australia lost 1.4 per cent.

Higher oil prices push inflation upward, and the main event for Wall Street this week will likely be Wednesday’s update on how bad inflation was last month. title: From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection
text:
Advertisement

MoneyInvestingCollectables From $1000 to half a million: How to build a valuable art collection Dan F Stapleton August 11, 2026 — 11:08am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In May, a painting by the abstract expressionist Mark Rothko fetched a staggering $US85.8 million ($120.8 million) at a Sotheby’s auction in New York. The result – the second-highest price ever paid for a Rothko at auction – made headlines. But what is arguably more remarkable is the painting’s ownership history, or provenance. The Emily Kam Kngwarray exhibition from the National Gallery of Australia. NGA The last time the Rothko changed hands, in 2003, Goldman Sachs banker Robert Mnuchin paid $US6.7 million for it. He held on to the work until his death late last year. For Mnuchin’s estate, the recent sale represents a gross return of more than 1100 per cent. It’s not the only example of artwork appreciating dramatically in a relatively short period of time. Here in Australia, works by the late, great Emily Kam Kngwarray regularly fetch $500,000 or more through dealers or at auction.

Advertisement

When they were painted, in the 1990s, they generally sold for a few thousand dollars each. Of course, not every artist’s reputation – and, correspondingly, the value of their work – grows over time. But if you have the opportunity to buy a painting by an artist on the ascent, should you? Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value. Art as an asset class It’s important to bear in mind that, to make money selling art, the resale price needs to be significantly higher than the price you paid. Dealers and auction houses generally charge commissions of between 25 and 35 per cent to sell work on a collector’s behalf, dwarfing the commissions charged by brokers of other asset types.

Advertisement

They can do this because art is a niche asset with a relatively small buyer pool. Often, sellers must rely on their brokers’ pre-existing relationships with buyers to secure sales. In Australia, those selling art on the secondary market must also pay the resale royalty: a 5 per cent fee collected by the government-run Copyright Agency and remitted to the artist or their estate. Finally, sellers must pay tax. The ATO classes art as a ‘collectable’, making it subject to the same capital gains tax (CGT) rules as most other assets. That means those reselling art after July 1, 2027 will receive an inflation-based discount, rather than the current 50 per cent CGT discount, and will be taxed at a minimum rate of 30 per cent. Reading the market Of the thousands of artists who sell artworks through galleries or online platforms each year, only a handful see their work appreciate in value.

Advertisement

Predicting which artists will rise is not an exact science, but certain conditions make price growth more likely, says D’Lan Davidson, whose D’Lan Galleries has outposts in Melbourne, Sydney and New York. Editor's pick Collectables Forget nostalgia: Why edgy Australian photography is suddenly worth a fortune “Signs to watch for are major exhibitions, museum acquisitions, strong curatorial interest, inclusion in important private collections and secondary-market demand.” Davidson gives the example of Kngwarray’s 2025 retrospective at Tate Modern in London. “That show ignited Emily’s market globally,” he says. Another way to identify artists with strong prospects is to familiarise yourself with the rosters of major commercial galleries.

Advertisement

“If an artist is strongly supported by a well-respected gallerist, there is a much better chance the work will have a broader market appreciation also,” Davidson says. Aspiring art collectors should proceed slowly and prioritise quality over quantity, he adds. “Even if it means buying fewer works, you should always buy the finest artwork that you can afford, from artists with a strong and consistent practice, impeccable provenance and real demand from serious collectors and institutions.” Works by Mark Rothko included in the Taubman Collection sale at Sotheby’s in New York. Reuters For love or money Many art collectors buy impulsively, motivated by dopamine and a fear of missing out, but circumspect buyers tend to build better collections, Davidson says.

Advertisement

Learning more about the artists and art movements that interest you is important, too, as it can help you accurately identify gems within a particular artist’s oeuvre. “The strongest collections are usually built with conviction, patience and knowledge,” Davidson says. Of course, the best reason to buy a piece of art is because you love it – and following your heart might be as good a money-making tactic as any. “In all my experience, and in a very strange way, artworks that have been adored generally resell for much better prices than artworks that have been stored away and never treasured,” Davidson says. title: MP calls for change to voluntary assisted dying law
text:
Independent MP Kate Chaney is trying to force debate in parliament on her proposal to let doctors give voluntary assisted dying (VAD) care over the phone.

Doctors cannot advise patients on VAD remotely because of a 20-year-old law designed to stop suicide being encouraged online.

Health professionals overwhelmingly back amending the law, including the Australian Medical Association, arguing it restricts support for patients too ill to travel or those living in remote areas.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Chaney's private member's Bill proposes a one-line amendment to the Criminal Code specifying that VAD is not suicide.

She said on Tuesday the tweak would "not alter any of the stringent safeguards established under state and territory VAD laws, or the clear clinical and professional standards for telehealth".

Independent MP Kate Chaney is trying to force debate on telehealth support for voluntary assisted dying. Picture: Supplied

"Today I am giving the government the opportunity to make good on the commitment made at the ALP national conference to remove barriers to the use of telehealth for voluntary assisted dying," she said.

"Labor says this is a matter for a conscience vote.

"And there is no reason for further delay, which only extends the needless suffering for people seeking dignity and choice at the end of their lives.

"The parliament should be allowed to debate and vote on my Bill that is ready to go."

title: Work-from-home laws delayed as premier eyes 'reset'
text:
Australian-first work-from-home laws have been delayed as Victoria's new premier hits the reset button on the state government's frayed relationship with the business community.

Premier Ben Carroll announced the move on Tuesday, confirming the start date for the proposed legal right would be pushed back from September 1 to July 2027.

The legislation would give full-time, part-time and casual workers the right to work from home two days a week on a pro-rata basis where reasonable.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Mr Carroll said he had communicated the change to Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Sally Curtain and Australian Industry Group's Victoria head Tim Piper.

Ben Carroll says he will work with the business community on the work-from-home laws. (James Ross/AAP PHOTOS)

Debate on the bill, which has already passed the lower house and was expected to pass the upper house this week, has also be delayed.

"I want to be very clear, I support work from home," Mr Carroll told reporters.

"I support flexible work. It is good for working families. I want to reset our relationship with the business community.

"That is why I've delayed these changes, and it's why I'm going to continue to work with the business community on making sure this policy is right."

Business lobby groups want the Victorian government's proposed work-from-home laws binned. (Lukas Coch/AAP PHOTOS)

The bill would still be passed before the November state election, the premier said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It has attracted staunch opposition from business lobby groups, which have called for it to be scrapped altogether.

Among the more contentious elements of the legislation is a requirement for employers to pay any reasonable costs to allow an eligible employee to work remotely.

Mr Carroll flagged he was keen to make "sensible amendments" and said he wanted to send a signal that Victoria was open for business.

"My door will always be open to the business community," the premier said.

title: State’s huge move on WFH reforms
text:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has delayed the state's work-from-home reforms until July next year.

In a press conference on Tuesday morning, Mr Carroll said the work-from-home reforms "would not proceed" on September 1 as expected and would instead be pushed out until July 1, 2027.

The proposed changes, which were introduced by ex-premier Jacinta Allan, would give eligible workers the right to work from home two days a week if it was reasonable to do so.

Ben Carroll has delayed work-from-home reforms. Picture: NewsWire / David Geraghty

Mr Carroll said while he still supported working from home,he said he "equally" wanted to continue working with the business community to ensure the policy was right.

"We need to make sure our economy – everyone knows it's a partnership between working families and the business community, and the government," he said.

"My door will always be open to the business community.

"I want Victoria to be open for business, I want it to be thriving."

He said the reforms 'would not proceed' on September 1 as expected. Picture: NewsWire / Luis Ascui

The proposed work-from-home Bill has faced criticism from business owners, including the Business Council of Australia, which urged for the reforms to be scrapped in favour of focusing on "turning around the Victorian economy, creating jobs and lifting living standards".

"This Bill is a solution trying to find a problem that does not exist because flexible work is already widely available across Victorian workplaces," the council said on Monday.

"Employers and employees already negotiate flexible arrangements that reflect the needs of individuals, their roles and their workplaces."

On Tuesday, Mr Carroll said the delay would offer the party more time to "make sure this policy is right".

"That's why I'm going to continue with the business community and make sure this policy is right," he said.

Mr Carroll previously said he would consider 'sensible' changes to he proposed legislation. Picture: NewsWire / David Geraghty

"I will study, I will listen and I will consult on any commonsense amendments."

On July 30, Mr Carroll said he would consider "sensible" changes to the upcoming legislation but would still enshrine the right to work from home for two days per week.

"Work from home does work for families, and now it will go through that parliamentary process, and we will consider anything that is sensible," he said at the time.

"Sensible changes will always come up in any debate, and like any other debate, they will be considered."
